title: How do you solve a cost reduction case from start to finish, with a fully worked example?
description: The complete cost reduction case guide: mapping the cost base, sizing levers against a 15% target in a bank, the mistakes to avoid and practice prompts.
hook: Cost cases are less about clever ideas and more about discipline: find where the money goes, attack the biggest lines, and check that each cut does not hurt revenue. Here is a worked example that hits a specific target.
body:
In this guide

  • When you will meet this case
  • The structure, and the first question to ask
  • A fully worked example with real numbers
  • The mistakes that cost candidates this case
  • Phrases to use
  • Practice prompts with model answers

When you will meet this case

The client needs to cut costs, often by a target percentage.

The structure

Which costs are in scope, and what must not suffer (quality, safety, service)?
  • Need less
    • Stop the activity (close a branch · move to self-service)
    • Do less of it (lower a service level, like free delivery)
  • Use less per unit
    • Cut waste and rework
    • Get more output per person or machine
  • Pay less per unit
    • Switch to cheaper inputs or outsource (rail instead of air freight)
    • Negotiate better prices

Cost = how much we do × resources per unit × price per resource. Each branch cuts one factor. Start with the biggest cost lines, and protect the costs that bring in revenue.

A fully worked example

The prompt: a retail bank spends £1B a year on operating costs and wants to cut 15%, or £150M, in two years.

Step 1: map the cost base. Branches £300M, IT £250M, back office £200M, call centres £150M, other £100M.

Step 2: size realistic levers on the biggest lines.

AreaLeverSaving
Branches (£300M)Close the 20% with the lowest footfall£60M
Call centres (£150M)Move 30% of calls to app and chat£45M
IT (£250M)Consolidate suppliers, cut 10%£25M
Back office (£200M)Automate routine processing, cut 10%£20M
Total£150M

Step 3: check what each cut does to revenue. Branch closures may lose some customers, especially older ones, so pair them with better digital support. Call-centre savings only work if the app actually handles those queries.

Recommendation: "We can reach £150M through four levers, with branches and call centres providing 70% of it. I'd protect revenue by closing branches only where digital use is already high, and start with IT and automation, which carry the least customer risk."

The mistakes that cost candidates this case

  1. Brainstorming cuts before mapping where the money actually goes.
  2. Spreading effort evenly instead of focusing on the biggest cost lines.
  3. Cutting costs that bring in revenue, like sales staff or service quality.
  4. Not checking whether the levers add up to the target.

Phrases to use

Before suggesting cuts, I'd like to see the cost base by category so we can focus on the biggest lines.
Branches and call centres give 70% of the target, so that's where I'd focus first.

Practise with these prompts

A fashion retailer's online returns now cost $40M a year, double three years ago.

Show a model structure
  • Number of returns: Online orders: did sales grow?; Return rate by category, size, brand; serial returners
  • Cost per return: Shipping, handling, refurbishing; Items that can no longer be sold
  • Why customers return: Fit and sizing, photos and descriptions; Ordering several sizes on purpose
  • Policy: Free returns, return window; Charging, store returns, exchanges first

Where to start: Orders × return rate × cost per return: find which grew, then the categories driving it.

The trap: Listing policies to change without first splitting the number of returns from cost per return.

A retail bank wants to cut operating costs by 15% in two years.

Show a model structure
  • Branches: Number, size and use of branches; Staffing vs footfall
  • Operations: Back office: payments, lending, account opening; Automation and outsourcing
  • Technology: Old systems, licences, data centres; Duplicate apps and vendors
  • Support functions: HR, finance, procurement; Spans of control and layers

Where to start: The biggest cost pool first: usually staff in branches and operations.

The trap: Listing cost ideas without sizing the cost base, so you can't say which matters.

A food-delivery start-up is burning $5M a month. Where would you cut?

Show a model structure
  • Unit economics per order: Commission, delivery fee, courier cost; Discounts and refunds
  • Marketing: Cost to acquire a customer vs their value; Promotions with no repeat
  • Cities: Profit by city; Exit or pause the weakest
  • Fixed costs: Head office, tech, offices; Hiring plans

Where to start: Profit per order by city: losing money on every order can't be fixed with volume.

The trap: Cutting head office first when the loss is in every order.
